checkpoints: Multer's default `FileInterceptor` uses memory storage, so the entire file is already sitting in `file.buffer` before the handler body runs; re-uploading that same buffer through `PutObjectCommand` doubles the bandwidth per upload, since bytes cross two legs — client→server, then server→storage.

Per-request RAM cost is roughly equal to the uploaded file's size, so N concurrent uploads hold N × filesize in heap at the same time — this is why OOM tracks concurrency under load, not average traffic volume.

The request holds an event-loop tick and the underlying connection for the full duration of the transfer (seconds to minutes for large files), which makes the API tier's connection/thread capacity — not CPU — the real throughput ceiling, and explains why P99 balloons under concurrent load.

Removing the server from the data path means replacing the proxy handler with a presign endpoint: the server generates a collision-free key and signs a short-TTL PUT URL via `getSignedUrl` with `PutObjectCommand`, the client PUTs the bytes directly to S3/MinIO, and storage validates the HMAC-SHA256 signature itself — server cost per upload drops from the full transfer time to sub-millisecond signing, with no buffer and no held connection.

Since a presign endpoint with no auth check would sign URLs for anyone who asks, authentication has to move into a guard that runs before `createUploadUrl` is called, rather than being implicit in the old handler.

A declared `size` field on the presign request is otherwise unsigned and uncapped for the whole TTL window, so it must be validated server-side on the request DTO to re-establish the size limit the old buffering handler enforced implicitly.

Signing `ContentType` as part of the presigned request causes a mismatched `Content-Type` header on the client's PUT to be rejected with 403 by storage, restoring the type check the proxy handler used to perform before forwarding to S3.

The bucket's CORS policy must explicitly allow `PUT` from the client's origin, or a browser's direct upload fails before a single byte reaches MinIO/S3 — a requirement that didn't exist when the server was proxying every request.

Because a completed request through the old handler used to double as proof that an upload happened, taking the server out of the data path introduces a new failure mode: a client that never confirms leaves an orphan object in storage, which needs a confirmation callback or a lifecycle rule on a `temp/` key prefix to clean up.
